title: Disciples matched to sicknesses and Luke as physician
english: “to the authorities in the heavenly places through the church the manifold wisdom of God” (Ephesians 3:10). Consider the wisdom of the Master. He chose his disciples for himself from every science and craft: Peter from fishermen, Matthew from tax collectors, Paul from tentmakers, and Luke from physicians. He did this not by chance and not without purpose. Humanity lay in the depth of error, and fishermen were needed. The devil had taxed Adam and robbed him of immortality, and an evangelist who was a tax collector was needed. Disobedience had clothed mankind in tunics of skin, and a tentmaker was needed, with grace to cut away the deadness of the passions with the knife of the divine Word.

The human race lay sick with many diseases: with the fever of debauchery, with the envy of greed and pleasure, with the despair that comes from the evil eye, and with the folly of idolatry. So Christ set Luke over them as a proven physician, and Paul cries out, “Luke the physician greets you” (Colossians 4:14). For Luke is truly a physician of souls. Do you want to see his workshop? Look at heaven. Do you want to see his practice? Look at his journey through the whole world. Do you want to see his store of drugs? Look at his surgery on Jewish tongues. Do you want to see his healing herbs? Look at the many different cures. Do you want to see the sick whom he visits? Look at the heretics next door. On one side those who reject the Spirit are sick with blasphemy, and on the other those who reject the Son are diseased with denial of God. Yet to both he prescribes what each needs, as a physician should. To the first Luke says, “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 4:30), and to the second he cries, “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father” (John 5:23). Luke is truly a great physician.

Do you want to see his skill? Look at the divine Gospel. The other evangelists told their story in one manner. What I mean is this. Matthew began from the genealogy according to the flesh, saying, “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1). Mark also proclaimed the plan of salvation according to the flesh, saying, “Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee” (Mark 1:9).
baehrens: PG 93; In sanctum Lucam (Khazarzar) u01 rem early
translator_notes: The text appears to be a fragment, starting mid-sentence with 'The church, situated in the heavenly realms…' and ending abruptly with '…but John alone proclaimed the unborn and unwitnessed birth.', which may indicate that it is part of a larger work.
The quotes 'The book of the genesis of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham' and 'Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee' are from Matthew 1:1 and Mark 1:9, respectively.
The quotes 'Do not grieve the Holy Spirit' and 'He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father' are allusions to Ephesians 4:30 and John 5:23, respectively.
orientation: The preacher is still laying out why Christ chose Luke the physician alongside Peter, Matthew and Paul.

title: John tells the eternal birth, Luke tells the whole mystery
english: John, the eagle among evangelists and lyre that speaks of God, proclaimed only the generation without beginning and without witness, and existence together eternal. Let the mouths of those who love insults be stopped, for the Son alone was begotten from the Father alone, and the generation above is without witness. No time was there, for he himself is the maker of all ages. No angel was there, for he himself is the one “who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flaming fire” (Psalm 104:4). No heaven was there, for “by the divine Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm” (Psalm 33:6). No sun was there, for he himself is “the sun of righteousness” (Malachi 4:2). No moon was there, for “the moon and the stars he himself founded” (Psalm 8:3). No earth was there, for he himself said, “Let the waters be gathered together and let the dry land appear” (Genesis 1:9). The generation above is therefore without witness, divine and beyond all understanding, since the Father alone knows how he begot and the Son alone knows how he was begotten. So John alone proclaimed the generation without beginning and existence together eternal.

But blessed Luke, the chosen treasure among evangelists and trader in this wondrous stone and precious pearl, the sleepless guard of the city, the skilled physician of souls, and the unbreached wall of kings, told the whole mystery together at once. He told of Gabriel’s good news, the reverence of the Virgin Mary, the visitation of the Holy Spirit, the form of God, the impassible self-emptying of his divinity, the unchanging and unconfused incarnation, the inviolate virginity, the sudden conception, and the incorrupt birth. He told of the angel’s announcement to the Virgin Mary, when he said, “Rejoice, favored one, the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28).

O greeting that suited no one else except the holy Virgin Mary alone. Eve gave birth, but in sorrows. Sarah gave birth, but in pain. Rebecca gave birth, but in groanings. Hannah gave birth, but in tears. Elizabeth gave birth, but in corruption. They all gave birth in sorrows because they all conceived in corruption. But you alone rejoice, gate of God and cloud of mystery. You alone rejoice, temple that holds the one whom nothing can contain. You alone rejoice, for the one who takes flesh from you “has taken away every tear from every face” (Isaiah 25:8).
translator_notes: The Greek text is a fragment, beginning mid-sentence and ending mid-sentence.
The translation of 'συναχθήτω τὰ ὕδατα' is 'let the waters be gathered', which is an imperative mood.
The translation of 'ὀφθήτω ἡ ξηρά' is 'appear the dry land', which is an imperative mood.

orientation: Hesychius has set out how Matthew and Mark began, and now contrasts John's proclamation of the eternal generation with Luke's full narration of the incarnation.

title: Only the Virgin rejoices, and Luke rests in Thebes
english: You alone rejoice, mother and heaven, maiden and cloud, the Virgin Mary and throne. As mother you bore the one who is from you and before you and with you. As the Virgin Mary you conceived the divine Word and labored to bring forth a mystery. As throne you carried in the womb him whom no one limits in his essence.

For this reason the prophet Isaiah stood in awe at the virginal mystery and cried out, “A voice of crying from the city, a voice from the temple was heard” (Isaiah 66:6). But what are you saying, O prophet? The riddle is firm and its meaning is deep. Isaiah calls John the voice, and he means the leaping in the womb by the cry. He names Elizabeth the city, and he proclaims the cave the temple. A voice of crying was heard saying, “Before she who was in labor gave birth, before the pain of labor came, she escaped and bore a male child” (Isaiah 66:7). The prophet took in the whole mystery at once, its swiftness and its birth and its virginity and its wonder, for the child came from no union. Isaiah says, “Before the pain of labor came,” for holy Mary did not suffer what Eve suffered. Isaiah says, “She escaped and bore a male child,” for grace did not wait for the limits of nature. The mystery of the plan of salvation keeps no set date.

So then, “Rejoice, favored one, the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28). For our Lord Jesus Christ has opened the arms of his welcome. He brings apostles into the bridal chamber, and he brings evangelists to completion. From them he established blessed Luke as speaker and teacher of the church.

This thrice-blessed evangelist Luke was Syrian by birth and physician by craft. He became a disciple of the apostles, and later he accompanied Paul until Paul’s martyrdom. After that he served the Lord without distraction and preached the word. Adorned with every virtue and shining with divine gifts, he fell asleep at eighty-four years of age in Thebes, the chief city of Boeotia, full of the Holy Spirit. He wrote the Gospel, showing through his preface that other accounts had been written before him and that believers from the Greeks needed an exact narrative of the plan of salvation set out for them. The holy evangelist Luke came to his rest on the eighteenth of October, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory and might, together with the immortal Father and the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
translator_notes: The translation aims to convey the meaning of the text in a natural and literary style, while remaining faithful to the original Greek.
The number '3' at the end of the text is likely an editorial note or a page number and has been omitted from the translation.
The Greek text may be fragmented, and some sentences may be cut off at the edges.

orientation: Hesychius finishes his praise of Luke by reading Isaiah as prophecy of the virginal birth and then recounting Luke's origin, Gospel, and death.
